paras: The threatened lynching of David James took place on August 7, 1903, in Camden, "just across the river from Philadelphia," when a crowd of about 500 pressed on a constable holding a Black man and called for the prisoner to be hanged. Officials held the crowd off, and James was sentenced the same day to thirty days in the county prison, a term the magistrate doubled. The episode drew notice mainly because the Alexandria Gazette used it to accuse Philadelphians of hypocrisy about lynching.

James, who also went by the name Muldoon and was described as "a negro" and "colored," had been arrested on a charge of insulting Minnie Cromheimer, a white woman. He was in the custody of Constable Christman when a crowd began to collect.

As the crowd grew, it was "whispered about" that the prisoner had attempted to assault a woman, a charge more serious than the one on which he had been arrested. Several men in the crowd then yelled "Lynch him!" and "Don't let him live," and the mob pressed forward, so that the constable had much difficulty keeping James from them. Game Warden Guthridge and Squire Thompson arrived and quieted the crowd.

James was then led to the squire's office for a hearing on the insult charge. Sentenced to thirty days in the county prison, he "became so defiant" that Justice Thompson doubled the sentence. No report of arrests among the crowd, or of any later proceedings, appears in the coverage.

The story reached print as a Philadelphia telegraph dated August 7, which the New-York Tribune ran on its front page the next day under the headline "MOB THREATENS NEGRO. Camden Crowd Wants to Lynch Him—Protected by Constable." The Tribune gave the dispatch without comment, describing an "infuriated mob of 500 Camdenites" and crediting the constable and the two officials with protecting the prisoner.

The Alexandria Gazette, on the same day, folded the dispatch into an editorial paragraph that began with a recent lynching in Delaware of a Black man accused of assaulting and murdering a white girl. Philadelphians, the Gazette wrote, had been "the loudest in their denunciation of the lynching," yet a mob of 500 "just across the river" had now threatened to hang a man arrested only for an insult. It closed that "it seems to be the verdict throughout the entire country that white women shall be protected from negro brutes," treating the Camden crowd as proof of a national consensus rather than as a threat to a prisoner.
No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press, and no local Camden or New Jersey account was found.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of David James
bases: A crowd of about 500 threatened to hang a Black prisoner in a constable's custody, shouting "Lynch him!", but did not take or harm him (A1, A2).

The mob of about 500 threatened to lynch James over an accusation of insulting, and a rumor of attempting to assault, a white woman, but the constable kept him from them and he was sentenced in court, so no one was killed (A1, A2).
Both reports carry the same Philadelphia dispatch, the Alexandria Gazette repeating its wording almost word for word, so there is one underlying account and no denial (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Philadelphia wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of 500 threatened to hang James after a rumor spread that he had attempted an assault; the constable held him until a game warden and the squire quieted the crowd, and he was sentenced to thirty days, doubled for defiance.

accounts.label: Alexandria Gazette editorial
accounts.gist: Retells the dispatch to contrast Philadelphia's denunciation of a recent Delaware lynching with a Camden mob 'just across the river', and concludes that the country agrees white women must be protected.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'MOB THREATENS NEGRO' and credited the constable with protecting the prisoner, without comment on the charge or the crowd.
The Alexandria Gazette used the episode against Philadelphia critics of lynching and closed that 'white women shall be protected from negro brutes.'
